We find that temporal validity is more important than simply retaining more history; specialty-factorized memory reduces context but can hide shared evidence; and multiple agents help when specialists must reason together, not merely when evidence comes from multiple memories. Guided by these findings, we propose \textit{MedCache}, a hybrid framework that constructs temporally valid patient memory, organizes evidence into overlapping specialty views, routes each query to relevant memories, and adaptively invokes one or multiple specialists. Experiments show that MedCache improves reasoning accuracy and memory efficiency over strong single-agent and multi-agent baselines, while generalizing across model backbones and external datasets.
item.dc:creator: Hei Ting Chan, Chenwei Wu, Xueshen Liu, Boyuan Zheng, Liyue Shen, Jiasi Chen, Z. Morley Mao

item.title: Trading Agents or Market Crashers? Dissecting Robustness and Security Failures in Academic Financial LLM Trading Schemes
item.description: arXiv:2609.19705v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents already trade real capital, and builders copy a few published designs that share models and news feeds, so one shock reaches many agents at once. We present FARSIGHT (Financial Agent Robustness and Security Investigation and Global Holistic Taxonomy), a systematization that rates trading agents on robustness to market stress and on security against source manipulation, agent compromise, and agents acting as attackers, and checks the ratings against released code. Across 15 academic schemes, no paper describes a halt that skips LLM inference or combines source provenance with cross-source corroboration, and the 7 code releases enforce no stop-loss or position limit outside the LLM. Three LLMs sell whole positions on a fake headline and on real hoaxes, including the fake press release behind the 2000 Emulex crash. In a simulated market driven by these decisions, one fake headline crashes the market in all runs with 400 agents, and 400 agents that sell when prices fall nearly double a 2010-sized crash. The pause that U.S. exchanges apply to large stocks starts in no headline run, whereas automatic halts and hard loss limits outside the model remove both effects. Restated as a domain-independent threat model, FARSIGHT maps the same gaps onto agents in healthcare, law, software, and crypto, where compromised agents spread harm as worms and as cascades. We derive 14 open problems and urge deployers to corroborate sources, keep interrupts that bypass the model, and enforce loss limits outside it.
item.dc:creator: Mengxiao Wang, Nitesh Saxena

item.title: Scam Town: Can Scam Education Spread Like a Vaccine?
item.description: arXiv:2610.25040v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Most older adults who hear a warning about scams hear it from someone they know: a relative, a neighbour, or a friend who was targeted. Yet research on scam prevention almost always studies one person at a time. We ask whether scam awareness can spread through a community and protect it the way a vaccine does, since a warning protects whoever hears it and can be passed on. To find out, we built Scam Town, a simulated community in which a large language model plays each resident. Scam centres phone the residents, and after a call a resident can warn the people they know. Word of mouth helped, but it did not take off on its own: each warning led to fewer than one more, so a community cannot count on warnings "going viral". Across 80 simulated towns, everyday talk cut the number of people scammed by roughly a fifth. The largest gains came when an official warning, from a bank, a senior centre, or an agency, reached most of a town and residents then talked about it: in simulation (a combination we did not test live) the two together cut scams by about half. Protection was greatest when warnings reached the people scammers actually call, who here were older residents. Because our residents are language-model stand-ins rather than real people, we treat these findings as predictions to test with people, not as proof. They point to a simple recipe for scam education: give people a clear story they can retell, design campaigns to be passed along, and reach first those most likely to be called.
item.dc:creator: Simiao Ren, Tommy Duong, Xingyu Shen, Jiaqi Gan, Tsang Ng, Ankit Raj, Kidus Zewde, Huaiyu Guo, Siyu Zhang

item.title: Distributed Swarm Morphogenesis with Neural Cellular Automata
item.description: arXiv:2610.31900v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Swarm morphogenesis requires robots to assemble desired shapes through local interactions. We present a modular framework integrating neural cellular automata (NCA) with existing site assignment and collision-aware control. Within this framework, we introduce a decentralized attachment-site discovery mechanism. Robots already in the formation update and share local NCA states to identify new attachment sites, enabling progressive growth without a predefined list of sites during deployment. To bridge the mismatch between conventional NCA growth and gradual physical assembly, we additionally propose offline sparse-retention fine-tuning that simulates partial attachment, together with a false-positive loss that penalizes invalid site activations. Simulations demonstrate formation of diverse lattice morphologies, scaling to several hundred robots, and substantial improvements in morphology accuracy from the proposed fine-tuning. Experiments with Crazyflie quadrotors validate the integrated execution pipeline using robot-relative observations reconstructed from external tracking.
item.dc:creator: Ray Verma, Eliseo Ferrante, Anthony Tzes
